title: The Canine Inventor's Workshop
clue: Ten minutes, one ordinary object, and the dog does all the thinking.
reveal: Welcome to the Canine Inventor's Workshop. Put a plain box on the floor and ask for nothing. Whatever your dog does with it, you reward and remember, and ideas that come back twice are filed as patents in your dog's name.
objective: Let your dog invent behaviors with one prop, reward the ones you want to see again, and file the repeats as patents.
instructions: Set up the lab: a non-slip floor, one sturdy shallow plain cardboard box, no tape or plastic (a shoebox lid or the bottom of a diaper box) and 15 to 20 tiny soft treats counted out of today's food. Nothing the box could trap a head or paw in.
Teach the marker first: pick a short word like 'yes' and say it, then hand over a treat, five times. Now the word means a treat is coming.

Open the lab: put the box down, sit, and say nothing else. The instant your dog looks at it, say your marker and toss a treat a step away so they have to come back and start fresh. Sniffing, pawing, stepping near, a nose touch: all count. Do not point, lure or hold anything out.

Raise the bar a crumb at a time: look, then nose touch, then paw, then a foot in or on the box. Pay only for the thing you want more of, and switch your target the moment they have done it three times. Rounds last one or two minutes, then a pause.
Watch for frustration: whining, barking at you, pawing at you or walking off. Make it easier (pay the previous step again) or end. A stuck dog is a stop sign, not a reason to push.
File the patents: any move repeated on their own three times gets a name ('Paw Sandwich', 'The Reverse Tuck') on a sticky note or your phone. Three patents is a big day. One is a good day.
Recess: after about ten minutes, take the box away and scatter a few treats across a towel so your dog can sniff them out slowly. That is the end of the session.
twist: You teach nothing and ask for nothing: your dog invents the tricks, you only say yes, and any invention that returns twice is filed as a patent.
variations: Easier: pay any contact with the box (a look, a sniff, a nose touch) and stop after five minutes.
Small-space version: use a hardcover book or a bath mat as the prop and work on a rug. No yard or extra room needed.
Harder: put a second prop (a low stool) next to the box and see whether your dog combines the two. Keep the box low and stable.
Toy instead of treats: reward with five seconds of play with a favorite toy, and let it go free whenever your dog drops it.
completion: It counts once you have said yes to one thing your dog did on their own. If your dog walks away, close the lab: that is a finished session too.
photoIdea: Your dog mid-invention with a nose or paw in the box, shot from floor level. No posing, just catch the thinking face.
memoryPrompt: What was the patent, and what did your dog do twice that surprised you?
supplies: Tiny soft treats from today's ration
dietNotes: Count the treats out of the day's food. Check labels for xylitol, and ask your vet if your dog has a restricted diet.
safety: Choose a prop that cannot trap a head or paw, and take it away if your dog starts tearing off pieces to swallow.
Keep rounds to a minute or two: a thinking dog gets frustrated before it looks it, so end on a success.
